reasons: Armenian anchor has kapeal + otiwkʻ, kapeal + jer̄awkʻ (instr. pl. of otn, jer̄n; ptcp. of kapem). Binding hand and foot is a universal restraint merism, and the Armenian (feet first, a prisoner handed over to torture in a martyr narrative) matches NT δήσαντες ... πόδας καὶ χεῖρας (Mt 22:13) and Jn 11:44, the obvious model for Christian Armenian prose. Generic and derivative.

The contexts differ (Russian narrative weather, Atharvan rain charm), and the OCR around the anchor is poor.

Two cognate body-part nouns, no verbal match, a universal restraint merism, and an NT model (Mt 22:13; Jn 11:44) for an Armenian martyr scene. The Sirens passages are voluntary restraint, a different context. Generic and derivative.

reasons: Anchor (Yeghishe 645, of Moses after he killed the Egyptian) has zmec anown dnēr nma. Martirosyan confirms anown < *h₁nómn̥ (s.v. anun) and dnem < *dʰeh₁-. Partners as cited: Od. 18.5 ὄνομ' ... θέτο, Od. 19.403 ὄνομ' ... θῆαι, RV 1.103.4d nā́ma dadhé (with śrávase 'for fame', close to Armenian name = renown), RV 1.72.3c nā́māni dadhire. Both members are cognate in the same verb–object relation, in naming/renown contexts. The grade rests on the native status of Arm. anun dnem: Martirosyan rejects a Greek calque (Gen 4:17 renders ἐπωνόμασεν; the phrase is found in dialects everywhere), so the grade does not depend on this witness. The passage itself paraphrases Exodus 2, and its 'great name' adjunct is biblical (Gen 12:2; see L011), so this witness is not independent proof.

known: Yes: PIE *h₁nómn̥ dʰeh₁- (Ved. nā́ma dhā-, Gk ὄνομα θέσθαι, Hitt. lāman dai-) is standard (Ivanov 1964ff., Mallory/Adams 1997: 438); Martirosyan (s.v. anun) cites Arm. anun dnem as its reflex.

reasons: Anchor (Agathangelos) has keal + zloys + tesanel ('to live and to see the light'). Martirosyan accepts tesanem < *derḱ- (*tersanem). loys (< *leuk-, Martirosyan) is not cognate with φάος. The Greek partners (Hipp. 1193 φάος δεδορκότας; 1163 δέδορκε ... φῶς) use δέρκομαι only occasionally, Homer's formula being ζώει καὶ ὁρᾷ φάος ἠελίοιο. What separates this from L010 is that the Armenian has the full coordinated structure of that formula, 'live and see light', as a definition of being alive, not the narrower 'have not seen light' = unborn. The Armenian is still equally explicable from Greek or biblical usage (Job 33:28; Ps 48:20 LXX) in a Hellenizing Christian text, and the light noun is renewed. One cognate element, with derivative risk.

reasons: Anchor (w1–w2): Jericho has seven walls; human nature is walled by aččʻawkʻ, akanǰawkʻ, r̄ngacʻn, beran (eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth), counted as seven. AVŚ 10.2.11 (sapta khāni ... karṇāv nāsike cakṣaṇī mukham) and 10.2.60 (nava dvārā ... pūr; 'pūr a yodhyā' = pūr ayodhyā) read as cited. The only cognate is the numeral seven, and counting the head's openings is plain anatomy. The Armenian is a biblical and patristic allegory (Jericho; the senses as gates), and the AV city has nine gates, not seven. Generic and derivative.

reasons: Anchor (Faustos) has martnčʻel + ordwocʻ + kanancʻ + ašxarhin (fight for children, wives and country, then churches and faith). kin ~ γυνή (*gʷénh₂) holds; nothing else is cognate. Il. 18.265 and Od. 11.403 have περὶ πτόλιος ... γυναικῶν as cited. Fighting for wives and children (and country) is a universal military topos and a Greek historiographic cliché (ὑπὲρ παίδων καὶ γυναικῶν; Lat. pro coniugibus ac liberis), available to Hellenizing Armenian prose; the Armenian has children where Homer has the city. One element only, and generic.

reasons: Anchor has ankaw + kʻown + canr + tʻanjramac, then tesanēr i teslean (a heavy, thick sleep fell on Basil and he saw a vision). Only kʻown ~ ὕπνος (*swep-; Martirosyan s.v. k‘un) is cognate; the 'heavy' adjectives are not. Theocritus 22.204 (an excluded late layer) has βαρὺς ἔδραμεν ὕπνος, of a dying man. Heavy sleep before a vision is a biblical motif (Gen 2:21, 15:12; Dan 8:18) and the evident model, and 'heavy sleep' is generic. Derivative and generic, in unlike contexts.

reasons: Anchor has auszra + ausztancze, beside saulelė + patekancze ('you will see the dawning dawn and the rising sun'). The same pairing recurs at 51485 (auszrös ausztanczės / saulelės patekanczös), so it is a daina formula. aušra (< *h₂eus-ro-, Derksen) and aũšti are inherited. reasons: Anchor has hateal + kʻown + yačʻacʻ ('sleep had been cut off from their eyes': the women at the tomb). kʻown ~ ὕπνος holds (Martirosyan s.v. k‘un); akn ~ ὄμμα (*h₃ekʷ-) is standard, though not re-checked. Il. 10.91 (ὄμμασι ... ὕπνος, negated) and Od. 5.492 (ὕπνον ἐπ' ὄμμασι χεῦ') read as cited, but neither has sleep leaving the eyes. The Armenian idiom is the biblical one of Gen 31:40 (LXX ἀφίστατο ὁ ὕπνος ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν): Mandakuni (xcl page 1198) uses kʻown + yačʻacʻn explicitly of Jacob's labours. Derivative, and also generic physiology.

reasons: Anchor has hataw + kʻown + yačʻacʻ + gišers ('sleep was cut off from his eyes for many nights': the anxious magus). Both nouns are cognate (kʻown/ὕπνος per Martirosyan; akn/ὄμμα standard). Esth 6:1, Dan 6:18), and Armenian authors use it with explicit reference to Jacob (Mandakuni page 1198). Derivative, and a widespread physiological metaphor.
